title: dentification of patient-specific molecular pathological mechanisms of reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and myocardial recovery potential in patients with aortic valve stenosis
summary:
Aortic valve stenosis is a common heart valve disease in which the aortic valve is narrowed, placing a greater strain on the heart. In some patients, the heart´s pumping function is also impaired. Although the narrowed valve can be treated with a catheter-based procedure (TAVI) or surgery (ACR), heart function does not recover to the same extent in all patients following treatment. The reasons for these varying outcomes are not yet fully understood.
The aim of this study is to investigate which biological changes in the heart muscle are responsible for the fact that the heart muscle recovers better in some patients than in others. To this end, a small tissue sample is taken from the heart muscle during treatment and examined in the laboratory.
In addition, clinical data, echocardiograms, cardiac MRI scans and blood test results are included in the study.
The findings are intended to help better predict in the future which patients are likely to benefit most from treatment and which mechanisms contribute to the recovery of heart function. In the long term, these results could contribute to the development of new, individually tailored therapies for heart failure.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1) Severe aortic valve stenosis
2) Reduced left ventricular systolic ejection fraction (<50%)
3) Indication for TAVI or AKE in accordance with current guideline recommendations or Heart Team consensus
4) Willingness to voluntarily participate in the study with a signed informed consent form
Exclusion criteria:
1) Known pregnancy at the time of enrollment
2) Life expectancy <1 year due to another non-cardiac condition
3) Prior TAVI or SAVR
4) Known myocarditis, infiltrative disease, or other primary non-valvular cardiomyopathies
